The left panel shows the clusters on the map of the first two principal components from Chapter 4 (Section 4.2.5), and the right panel the means of each cluster, in standard deviations:

pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

fig_states_clusters <- function(base = 13) {
  d <- tibble(x = st_pc$x[, 1], y = st_pc$x[, 2], abb = rownames(X6), cl = km_states$cluster)
  share <- st_pc$sdev^2 / sum(st_pc$sdev^2)
  map <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y, colour = cl)) + axes0 +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    geom_text_repel(aes(label = abb), size = 3.3, seed = 4, max.overlaps = 40, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = pal_states, name = NULL) +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(title = "The 50 states, by cluster",
         x = sprintf("PC1 score (%s of the variance)", pct(share[1])), y = sprintf("PC2 score (%s)", pct(share[2]))) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = base) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
  ctr <- as_tibble(km_states$centers, rownames = "cl") |> pivot_longer(-cl, names_to = "var", values_to = "z") |>
    mutate(cl = factor(cl, levels = c("South", "North", "Rest")), var = factor(var, levels = rev(vars6)))
  prof <- ggplot(ctr, aes(z, var, colour = cl)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
    geom_point(size = 3.2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = pal_states, guide = "none") +
    labs(title = "Cluster means", x = "standard deviations from the mean of all states", y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = base) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
  map + prof + plot_layout(widths = c(1.45, 1))
}

# draw the figure
fig_states_clusters()

The names come from the means. One cluster has low incomes, much illiteracy, short lives, a high murder rate, few graduates and little frost, and 11 of its 12 states lie in the South. Another has long lives, few murders, many graduates and much frost: these 18 states stretch across the North, from New England through the Midwest and the Plains to the Mountain West. The remaining 20 states, among them California, New York, Illinois and Florida, have the highest incomes and are close to the average otherwise.

Here no species tell us whether the clusters are real. One check is whether other methods find them too. Ward’s method gives the same three clusters, but it minimises the same \(W\) as k-means, so it is not an independent check. Average linkage and the mixture, with the number of groups chosen by BIC, give different answers:

name_states <- function(cl) {
  nm <- sapply(split(rownames(Z6), cl), function(s) {
    if (all(c("AK", "NV") %in% s) && length(s) == 2) return("Alaska and Nevada")
    km <- table(km_states$cluster[rownames(Z6) %in% s])
    if (km["South"] == length(s)) "South" else if (km["North"] == length(s)) "North" else
      if ("CA" %in% s && length(s) < 10) "West" else "Rest"
  })
  factor(nm[as.character(cl)], levels = names(pal_states))
}

fig_states_methods <- function(base = 13) {
  res <- list("k-means: three clusters" = km_states$cluster,
              "Average linkage: three clusters" = name_states(avg_states),
              "Mixture (BIC): five groups" = name_states(mix_states$classification))
  d <- purrr::map_dfr(names(res), function(m) tibble(x = st_pc$x[, 1], y = st_pc$x[, 2], abb = rownames(X6),
                                                     cl = res[[m]], method = factor(m, levels = names(res))))
  ggplot(d, aes(x, y, colour = cl)) + axes0 +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    geom_text_repel(data = filter(d, abb %in% c("AK", "NV", "CA", "FL", "HI")), aes(label = abb), size = 3.2,
                    seed = 2, show.legend = FALSE) +
    facet_wrap(~method) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = pal_states, name = NULL, drop = TRUE) +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(x = "PC1 score", y = "PC2 score") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = base) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = base))
}

# draw the figure
fig_states_methods()

Average linkage finds the same 12 states of the South, but it sets Alaska and Nevada apart as a cluster of two and keeps all other states together. The mixture finds five round groups (EII): the South and the North as in k-means, Alaska with Nevada, six states in the West and Florida (AZ, CA, FL, HI, OR, WA), and the remaining 12.

So the South is a group that every method finds, and so, apart from average linkage, is the North. How the other states are grouped depends on the method. Groups that do not depend on the method deserve more trust than groups that do, and a clustering method returns \(k\) clusters whether or not the data have them. The three clusters of k-means are a useful summary of the states, like their two factors in Chapter 6 (Section 6.8), rather than a discovery. Everitt and Hothorn (Section 6.4.1) reach a similar conclusion with k-means on the crime rates of the states: their two clusters split the states along the first principal component, and the analysis may only divide a homogeneous set of states in two.

Check your understanding
  1. Ward’s method gives the same three clusters of states as k-means. This is a weak check, because
    1. Ward’s method uses another distance
    2. both minimise the same within-cluster sum of squares \(W\)
    3. Ward’s method always gives three clusters
    4. k-means starts from the clusters of Ward’s method
  2. The same 12 states of the South form a cluster with every method. This suggests that
    1. the other clusters are just as trustworthy
    2. the South is a group in the data, not a product of one method
    3. there are exactly three groups of states
    4. the South has the most states
  3. Run with \(k=3\) on data without any groups, k-means
    1. reports an error
    2. still returns three clusters
    3. returns one cluster
    4. returns the principal components
Answers 1 b. 2 b. 3 b.

7.7 Clusters and factors

Factor analysis and model-based clustering are both models with a latent variable, and they share more than their form:

Factor analysis Model-based clustering
Latent variable continuous factors \(\mathbf f_t\) a discrete group \(g_t\)
Model \(\mathbf x_t=\Lambda\mathbf f_t+\mathbf u_t\) \(\mathbf x_t=\mu_{g_t}+\mathbf u_t\)
What it groups variables that load on the same factor observations that lie in the same hill
Not identified the turn of the factors the numbers of the groups
Estimates for each observation factor scores, never exact membership probabilities, never certain
How many? the likelihood ratio test BIC
A change of units rescales the loadings, not the factors rescales the means and covariance matrices, not the groups, if the shape can adapt

PCA and k-means are the model-free relatives: PCA looks for the directions of largest variance, k-means for compact clusters, and both depend on the units of the variables.

7.8 Summary

  • A cluster model has a discrete latent variable: observation \(t\) belongs to group \(g_t\), and \(\mathbf x_t=\mu_{g_t}+\mathbf u_t\). The centre jumps among \(k\) points, which can lie anywhere, while the centre of a factor model slides along a line or a plane. Cluster analysis estimates the groups from the observations alone.
  • Hierarchical clustering merges the two closest clusters, step by step. The dendrogram records the merges, and cutting it gives clusters. The linkage defines the distance between clusters: the closest pair (single, which can chain), the farthest pair (complete), the average of all pairs, or the rise in the within-cluster sum of squares \(W\) (Ward).
  • k-means minimises \(W\) for a given \(k\): assign each observation to the nearest centre, move each centre to the mean of its cluster, and repeat. It favours round clusters of similar spread, depends on the units, and can end in a local minimum, so it is run from many starts.
  • Model-based clustering fits a mixture of normal densities, \(f(x)=\sum_l\pi_lf_l(x)\), by maximum likelihood with the EM algorithm. Each observation gets membership probabilities, and each group an ellipse. BIC chooses the number of groups and their shape. k-means is the special case of round groups of equal size.
  • Standardise the variables before k-means or hierarchical clustering when their units differ. A mixture whose covariance matrices can adapt to the units does not need it.
  • For the penguins, the clusters match the species, and BIC even split the Gentoo by sex. For the states, only the South is found by every method. A clustering method always returns groups, so groups that several methods find deserve more trust than groups that depend on the method.

Cluster analysis finds groups of observations that lie together. A model for the groups adds membership probabilities, shapes for the clusters and a way to choose their number.

7.8.1 Further reading

  • Everitt and Hothorn (2011), An Introduction to Applied Multivariate Analysis with R, Chapter 6: hierarchical clustering (with body measurements and jet fighters), k-means (with the crime rates of the US states and Romano-British pottery), model-based clustering with finite mixtures (with a survey of European doctors on what they tell cancer patients), and displays of the clusters (neighbourhood graphs and stripes plots).
  • Everitt, Landau, Leese and Stahl (2011), Cluster Analysis, a book-length treatment.
  • Kaufman and Rousseeuw (1990), Finding Groups in Data: An Introduction to Cluster Analysis.
  • Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman (2009), The Elements of Statistical Learning, Section 14.3, on k-means, hierarchical clustering and mixtures.
  • Ward (1963) on Ward’s method, MacQueen (1967) and Lloyd (1982) on k-means, and Dempster, Laird and Rubin (1977) on the EM algorithm.
  • Fraley and Raftery (2002), “Model-based clustering, discriminant analysis, and density estimation”, and Scrucca, Fop, Murphy and Raftery (2016), “mclust 5”, on model-based clustering in R.
  • Gorman, Williams and Fraser (2014), “Ecological sexual dimorphism and environmental variability within a community of Antarctic penguins (genus Pygoscelis)”, the study behind the penguin data.
